const r=load("aes_detector_root");
const body=`# Clean AES detector results and retained-baseline comparison

All four original HT1–HT4 models completed inference on the professor-supplied clean AES reference and returned CLEAN, with zero of four Trojan votes. The retained recovered-baseline run also returned CLEAN, zero of four votes. **Both results classify approximate graphs; neither certifies complete hardware security or assignment completion.**

The AES run is new and isolated. The baseline was not rerun. No source changes, generation, training, adaptation to detector feedback, key work, published solutions or board operations were used.

## Numerical comparison

The following values are each classifier's P(Trojan) output, not calibrated probabilities of actual compromise.

| Model | Recovered baseline, retained | Clean AES, new | Prediction on both |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| HT1 | 0.07584280 | 0.04823842 | CLEAN |
| HT2 | 0.35516843 | 0.04757138 | CLEAN |
| HT3 | 0.21610928 | 0.16328798 | CLEAN |
| HT4 | 0.04644027 | 0.02378227 | CLEAN |

Clean AES P(clean): HT1 0.95176160, HT2 0.95242858, HT3 0.83671206, HT4 0.97621775. Mean P(Trojan) is 0.07072001 for AES versus 0.17339019 for the retained baseline. The supplied ensemble reports TROJAN if any model votes class 1; neither run had a positive vote.

All four model-load records, checkpoint/configuration hashes and the 37-feature vocabulary bytes match the baseline run exactly. Models ran on CPU with strict weights-only loading, evaluation mode, seed 0 and one thread. The log-softmax, argmax and ensemble calculations are unchanged.

The new process returned exit 0 with no timeout. Its only stderr was the ordinary first-use matplotlib font-cache notice.

[Machine-readable comparison](@ROOT@/COMPARISON.json), [new raw results](@ROOT@/runs/clean_aes_detection/RESULTS.json), [stdout](@ROOT@/records/detector.stdout), [command and exit record](@ROOT@/records/detector_command.json).

## Graph route and limitations

| Property | Recovered baseline | Clean AES |
|---|---|---|
| Graph route | Exact extraction failed, then built-in heuristic fallback | Direct large-lookup heuristic shortcut |
| Exact-extraction status | Failed on missing SBRAM404K definition | Not attempted under supplied default shortcut |
| Qualifying lookup rows | 0 | 512 |
| Graph nodes / edges | 5,728 / 10,947 | 835 / 1,121 |
| Weakly connected components | 1 | 3 |
| Operation labels | 2,880 generic branch | 513 branch, 17 xor, 4 concat |

The supplied notebook switches directly to its heuristic when at least 128 lookup-table rows are present. AES had 512, so this is the expected original detector path, not a newly introduced workaround. It does not establish exact graph extraction.

The heuristic concatenates text and extracts assignments. It does not fully elaborate hierarchy/instances, distinguish same-named signals in different modules, or represent case selection, control conditions, timing and sequential semantics. All three files being present therefore does not imply complete semantic coverage of AES. The retained baseline additionally lacks behavioral definitions of its four RAM primitives in detector input.

The new graph has 301 signal nodes and 534 operation nodes. These counts describe the heuristic representation, not gate counts or physical resource usage. Saved graph features are not proof that every HDL behavior was modeled.

The lower AES model scores are a descriptive observation, **not a security ranking** between the two designs. The designs, structures and graph routes differ; calibration, sensitivity and false-negative rates have not been measured by this comparison. Two reference classifications do not establish attack detection quality.
